**Short answer:** The vault has no churn benchmark from Hormozi, and nothing on when churn becomes a problem. It has one relevant story. In his paid community, Skool Games, the main reason people cancelled was overwhelm, not a lack of value, and he fixed it by delivering less. The rest of this answer is extrapolation from his principles.

**What he's said**
- He asks people why they cancelled and changes the product based on the answer: "the number one reason that people were cancelling was overwhelm. It was not oh I need to provide more value. It was I need to provide more value per second in fewer total seconds." ([Less is More, May 2025 @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s))
- **What he did:** he cut the weekly calls from three to one. He moved the big content drop from monthly to quarterly. He turned off app features so new members had fewer things to do: "Oh my god, there's so many things I have to do… And then they leave" (same video @ 11:35).
- His rule: "you only introduce something when it's required or necessary for that person to get the the desired value" (@ 11:35).
- He's against relying on a single community price. "even if you're on school, you have a community, you charge 100 bucks a month, whatever it is, have something that's $1,000 a month. Have something that's $10,000 one time." ([If I Started A Business in 2026, Dec 2025 @ 9:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=587s))
- More broadly: "do what you can control, make more from each one." ([My final update, 2025 @ 8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)). That line comes from an ad script for his book launch.

**Where this is uncertain:** The vault holds only 7 sources. He has very likely talked about churn and lifetime value elsewhere, but none of that material is in the vault, so I'm not quoting a figure he never said here. The Skool story also has no numbers attached: no churn rate, before or after.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the principles above, not his words)
- **Don't look for a "good" percentage. Look at what churn does to your ceiling.** He reduces things to inputs and outputs. Your community stops growing when the members leaving each month equal the members joining. So the most members you can reach is roughly new members per month ÷ monthly churn. With 100 joins a month, 10% churn caps you near 1,000 members, and 5% churn caps you near 2,000. Halving churn doubles the size of the business without spending more on ads.
- **Worry when:**
  1. You've stopped growing even though new members are still coming in. That means you've hit the ceiling above.
  2. People cancel in their first month. Read that as onboarding overwhelm, as in his Skool story.
  3. You don't know why people leave. He knew the top reason; you should too.
- **Fix churn by taking things away, not adding them.** People's instinct is to add bonuses and more calls. He'd say find the one thing most members value, get them to it fast, and hide everything else until they need it.
- **Make churn hurt less with your money model.** A $1k/month tier and a $10k one-time offer above the $100 community mean the members who ascend carry the economics. Losing $100 members matters less.

**Note:** for a numeric benchmark you'll need outside data, such as Skool's own stats or SaaS churn benchmarks. The vault doesn't support any number in his name. If you'd like to fill this gap, I can look for his videos that cover churn and LTV directly and add them to the vault.

I'd take the percentage of revenue. The vault has nothing where Hormozi talks about profit-share versus revenue-share pay, so that recommendation is my extrapolation from things he has said, not a quote.

**What the vault does have**

- **He grew revenue for years and made almost no profit.** He describes his gym business as going from "making a few million dollars a year in topl line revenue and basically no profit to millions and millions and millions of dollars a year in topl line and bottom line profit" by restructuring the offer ([source @ 1:24:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5089s)). So by his own account, a business can be busy and successful and still show no profit.
- **He lost everything on a partner's word.** He put all his gym-sale money into a launch with a partner. The next morning he checked the bank account: "it's completely empty." When he brought the bank statements to a meeting, the partner "pushed it off the table," and Hormozi then learned the partner "had already been indicted for fraud" ([@ 18:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1114s), [@ 19:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1146s)). His lesson: "when experience meets money money gets the experience and experience gets money" ([@ 19:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1179s)).
- **He wants cash collected early.** He describes the goal of a money model as "how do you pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion" ([@ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). That quote comes from a video promoting his own book.

**Extrapolation (my reasoning from those principles, not his words)**

- **The client decides what "profit" is.** They control salaries, the owner's pay, new hires, ad spend and the accounting. They can make your share shrink without doing anything wrong. Revenue is much harder to shrink and much easier to check.
- **Profit is the number that's easy to hide.** The bank-account story is a warning against getting paid from a number someone else controls and won't show you.
- **Revenue pays sooner.** You get paid on every sale. Profit is often calculated quarterly or yearly, after costs, if there is any.
- **Revenue matches what you actually affect.** Most consultants move offers, sales and marketing, which show up in revenue. You don't control costs, so don't get paid on them.

**When profit share could make sense:** if your job is mainly cutting costs or fixing margins, if profit is shared monthly from books you can audit, or if the profit percentage is several times higher than the revenue percentage (profit is usually a small part of revenue). A fair comparison is "X% of revenue vs. X% × margin of profit."

**What I'd actually do:** take the revenue percentage. Ask for a base retainer on top so you aren't working for free while things ramp up, and get written rights to see the sales data. That last part follows from his partner story.

**Where this is uncertain:** he never talks about how consultants should be paid. His own deals are equity: Acquisition.com takes ownership stakes in companies, which is closer to a profit share with control. He'd likely accept profit exposure if he also had ownership and could see the books.

**Short answer:** The vault has nothing where Hormozi talks about raising from investors versus bootstrapping. Everything he says about starting out is about funding growth with your own revenue. That means selling something expensive, often your own time, and using the cash to grow. Extrapolating from that, he'd almost certainly tell a first-time founder to bootstrap.

**What he's said**
- **Pay for growth with expensive one-on-one work.** In December 2025 he said one of the simplest first offers is to sell your own time one-on-one, "even if it's unscalable" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 1:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=66s)). He says it "doesn't have to be scalable" (@ [2:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=129s)), and that "If you trade your time for the money, you have a 100% margin" (@ [6:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=360s)). His recipe: "be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" (@ [15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s)).
- **Fix how you get paid before looking for outside money.** The point of a money model is to "pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion uh within a business so that you can scale" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). The goal is "to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better." If customers cost too much to get, "do what you can control, make more from each one" (@ [8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)). In another 2025 talk he gives "pull cash flow from 90 days to to 30 days" as an example of the one thing that could change a business ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=264s)).
- **Capital comes last in his sequence.** He says each jump in his monthly income came from adding a kind of leverage. The order was labor (self-employed, then staff), then media (licensing), and only then capital, which took him to eight figures a month ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:43:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6181s)).
- **Limit your downside.** "when you have a a capp downside, an uncapped upside, that is the recipe for opportunity" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 15:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=909s)).

**What he's done**
- At his first gym in Huntington Beach, he took on one personal-training client. That income covered his own living costs, so all the gym's money could go into growth ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 1:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s)).
- He rebuilt from $1,000 in December 2016 to Gym Launch, which he says did $26M top line and $17M EBITDA in its first 12 months. He describes it as funded by sales, not investors ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 21:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1279s), [@ 31:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1870s)).
- He did take outside money, but only at the exit. In 2021 he sold two-thirds of two of his companies to a private equity firm for $46.2M (@ [31:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1905s)).
- His first big loss had nothing to do with investors. He put his gym-sale money into a launch with a partner who had already been indicted for fraud, and the partner emptied the bank account (@ [18:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1114s)).

**Where this is uncertain**
- None of the vault's six sources (2023–2025) asks him directly about venture capital, angel investors or raising a seed round. He has never weighed the two options on the record here.
- **Conflict of interest:** Acquisition.com usually buys 25–49% minority stakes in businesses that are already profitable ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 32:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1972s)). So he is an investor himself, but in businesses that already make money, not early-stage ideas. "Bootstrap until you're profitable, then take a partner" also happens to be his own deal flow.
- The dollar figures in the personal-training story don't add up in the auto-captions. The point of the story is clear, but don't trust the numbers.

**Extrapolation** (not in the sources; my reasoning from the principles above)
- For a first business he'd likely say bootstrap. Get to cash flow fast with an expensive offer, even one-on-one work, so the business pays for itself. His stair-step ordering puts capital after you can already sell and deliver.
- He'd probably say outside money doesn't fix a weak offer or money model. If customers aren't saying yes, he says improve the offer, and if acquisition costs too much, make more from each customer. Raising money to cover either problem just loses more money, faster.
- His capped-downside rule, plus his own experience losing everything through a partner, suggests he'd be wary of giving away ownership or control in a first business.
- The likely exception: once you have a profitable business, bringing in capital as a partner is the stage he's at now. Note that this is exactly the kind of deal Acquisition.com does.
- The vault also has no evidence on businesses that need heavy capital before they can earn anything, such as deep tech or hardware. His advice may not apply there.

My own view, in one line: this bootstrap logic suits service and info businesses like his. For capital-heavy or winner-take-all startups, the venture-capital route is a separate question he doesn't address here.

**Short answer:** Nothing in the vault describes how Hormozi structures a workday, so the schedule below is my extrapolation. What his sources do give is a clear set of priorities. Your business doesn't make enough money, so most of your day should go to the one thing that would fix that, which is usually getting more customers or charging more per customer. Do it in high volume, let everything else slide, and work as many hours as you can while you're still producing.

**What he's said**

- **Decide what the one thing is before you plan the day.** The CEO's job is to name "what one thing if it were true 12 months from now would change everything for our business" ([2025 talk @ 3:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=232s)). If you can't name it, "I'm not doing my job and I need to think about it longer." Once you've chosen it, "sometimes you have to let the little fires burn" ([@ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)).
- **Break "make more money" down into concrete steps.** He does this himself: "I want to grow my business I'm like all right what does that mean like well get more customers make them worth more" ([DOAC 2023 @ 35:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2137s)). He also asks: "if you do not know the inputs that are going to get the output that you want then what are you doing" ([@ 38:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2338s)).
- **Volume matters more than polish.** He learned sales by doing as many reps as possible with quick feedback, and his advice is to "go Shadow the best guy and do twice the volume he's doing" ([@ 40:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2402s)). Reps shorten how long you stay bad at something "in terms of calendar days" ([@ 40:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2435s)).
- **Hours.** In 2023 he said, "I work until I can't work meaning like my put per unit of time starts to drop precipitously and then I know that I just need to take a break" ([@ 1:09:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4168s)). In 2025 he made it a recommendation: "if you're under 30 and you have no responsibilities, I recommend working as many hours per week as humanly possible" ([2025 @ 11:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=712s)).
- **Say no to new ideas.** "the effort that it takes to compound is the length of time you have to say no to everything else" ([@ 22:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1378s)).
- **If you need cash now, sell your time at a premium, but cap it.** "be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" ([Dec 2025 @ 15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s)).

**What he's done:** At his first gym he taught every class himself and then ran sales consults at 8, 9, 10 and 11 p.m. for about six months ([@ 55:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=3305s)). Another time he took on one cash-paying personal-training client to cover his own living costs, so all of the gym's money could go into growth ([@ 1:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s)).

**Where this is uncertain:** His views on how much to work are personal philosophy, not expertise. In 2023 he refused to tell others what they "should" do, and by 2025 he was recommending maximum hours. Even then he added conditions: the advice is for people who are unhappy where they are and have no responsibilities. If you have kids, he says there are trade-offs ([@ 12:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=744s)). Some of these videos also promote his own funnel.

---

**Extrapolation (my reasoning from the principles above, not something he said)**

1. **Start each week by naming the one constraint.** Write down the single number that would change everything, such as "2× more sales calls booked" or "average order value from $X to 3X." If you can't pick one, he'd say you haven't thought about it long enough.
2. **Spend the first and largest part of the day on that one thing, with a daily volume target.** That means outreach, sales calls, ads or content, or improving the offer. Set a number of inputs, like 100 messages or 5 calls, so the day is about reps and not just being busy.
3. **Fit everything else into one short block at the end.** Admin, email, tweaking the website and small fires all go there. Anything that isn't the one thing can wait or stay a bit broken.
4. **If the money is tight, sell a premium one-on-one version and cap it at about 5–10% of your time.** Price it so it's clearly worth the hours, and put what it earns into the main business.
5. **No fixed end time.** Stop when your output drops, then rest. Only take this part literally if his conditions fit you: unhappy with where you are, and few responsibilities.
6. **Don't change direction every few weeks.** Keep the same one thing until you've hit it. New ideas go on a list for after that.

My own note: none of this comes from a schedule he actually described. It's built from his priorities, so treat the structure as a starting point and change it once your numbers show what's working.

**Short answer:** No source in the vault talks about paying down business debt versus keeping cash, so there's no direct quote to give you. The closest material points one way. A profitable service business carrying a moderate debt load is not, by his standards, "in the hole." He would most likely tell you to keep the cash and put it into whatever grows the business fastest. The exception is if the debt is expensive or is what keeps you up at night; then he'd tell you to clear it.

**What he's said (closest material)**
- **Get out of the hole first, then think long-term.** "I get that you can't have a vision if you have bills to pay, if rent is due… this is why I'm such an advocate of like get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible… Just get your head above water. At that point, options open up." ([2025, @ 17:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s)) He's talking about personal survival here, not business debt. Still, it's the test he'd apply: are you underwater or not? A profitable business with $60k of debt usually isn't.
- **Spend aggressively, but stay at break-even or better.** "the goal is to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([2025, @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). His goal is to "pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion… so that you can scale" (same source). Cash is something he puts to work, not something he holds onto.
- **Cover your needs, then go aggressive with the rest.** "make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" ([2025, @ 15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s)).
- **Capped downside, uncapped upside.** "when you have a a capp downside, an uncapped upside, that is the recipe for opportunity" ([2025, @ 15:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=909s)).
- **Pick one bet and don't spread your resources thin.** "me trying to solve it in two or three ways ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work" ([2025, @ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)).

**What he's done**
- In December 2016 a payment processor froze six months of his funds and he was down to $1,000 ([2023, @ 21:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1279s)). He then used a credit card with a $100,000 limit to cover about $3,300 a day in sales-team costs and launched six gyms anyway ([@ 22:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1345s)). That's debt used for growth, at his most desperate point. It worked, but it was a do-or-die bet, not a model he recommends.
- At his early gym, he took one cash-paying personal-training client to cover his own living costs. That let him reinvest all of the gym's money into growth ([2025, @ 1:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s)).

**Where this is uncertain**
- No source covers interest rates, debt payoff or cash reserves, so all of the above is inferred.
- His own story also argues for keeping cash: a payment processor froze his money and he nearly went under. Read that way, keeping a cash buffer matters as much as having profits.
- Several of these lines come from launch content that also sells his books and scaling programs (see the profile's conflicts of interest).

**Extrapolation** (reasoned from the principles above, not something he said)
1. **Can a dollar put into growth earn more than the debt's interest rate?** If $1 of marketing or sales spend brings back well over $1 within months, paying off cheap debt early slows you down. That follows from his idea of spending as much as possible while staying at break-even.
2. **Expensive debt is different.** For credit cards or merchant cash advances at 20%+, he'd probably say paying it off is a guaranteed return few growth bets beat. That fits "get out of the hole."
3. **Keep a buffer.** The processor freeze shows how fragile a business is when it has no cash on hand. Don't spend down to zero, whichever way you go.
4. **Fix the money model before borrowing more.** His 2025 framing would be to find ways to collect cash sooner from each customer, such as upfront payments or premium tiers. Then growth funds itself and the debt matters less.
5. **If the debt is pulling your attention away, clear it.** If it keeps you from focusing on your one big bet, his "one thing" logic says remove the distraction.

To sum up the extrapolation: if the debt is cheap and you have a growth channel with proven returns, keep the cash and grow. Then pay the debt down out of the extra profit. If the debt is expensive, pay it off.

My own note, outside the vault: the interest rate and how stable your monthly cash flow is decide this more than any philosophy. Check both before you act.

**Short answer:** Nothing in the vault gives a refresh schedule (weekly, every N days, etc.), and Hormozi never uses the phrase "ad fatigue" in any source here. What he does say goes against refreshing on a calendar. When a hook wins, keep running it as long as it works, and keep testing new hooks to try to beat it. Swap it out only when the numbers show a challenger has won.

**What he's said**
- **Keep a winner running and try to beat it:** "if you have a winning hook for your ad campaigns you keep using it to death and you try and beat it" ([yt-JDR-R--4HhM @ 1:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=73s), *14 Years of Marketing Advice in 35 Minutes*, 2025)
- **Hooks are where new versions pay off most:** "a banger or killer headline can absolutely outperform the control by two three sometimes 5x". He adds that most other changes in a funnel give "20% lift 50% lifts that'd be a monster split test" ([@ 0:36–1:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=36s)). His reasoning is that going from a 1% to a 3% click-through rate triples the number of people who see everything after the ad.
- **A new hook is new packaging on the same offer:** "the headlines serve to give us a different wrapping paper for the same offers" ([@ 1:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=111s)). Change the hook and leave the offer as it is.
- **Where to find new hooks:** "look at your organic content or other people's organic content or other people's ads look at the first 3 seconds visually and verbally", and "can I steal like an artist from a different industry" ([@ 1:51–2:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=111s))
- **The comedian's method of testing:** comedians try new material in many clubs, find the eight minutes that land, move those to the front, and keep testing the rest ([@ 34:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=2077s)). You can run ad copy the same way: keep what wins and keep testing new lines against it.

**What he's done:** During the August 2025 *$100M Money Models* launch, his team ran ads in high volume. They waited for data "so there's a little more statistical significance" and then made new creative based on it ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 2:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=167s), *My final update*). That line probably comes from a team member, not Hormozi, so it shows how his team worked rather than something he said himself. Either way, data set the timing, not the calendar.

**Where this is uncertain**
- The vault has no numbers on frequency, CPM creep, how often to rotate, or how many creatives to test per week.
- His copywriting checklist is a practitioner's list. By his own account he's "good enough" at copywriting, not a specialist. His credibility here comes from the scale of his ad spend (he says tens of millions a year across his portfolio companies).
- The talk the copy advice comes from also promotes his free scaling roadmap lead magnet.

**Extrapolation** (not in the sources)
- Don't ask "how often should I refresh?" Ask "is my control still winning, and do I have enough challengers in testing?" Keep a steady flow of new hooks against your best ad, and swap only when one wins by a meaningful margin.
- Treat fatigue as a signal in your numbers: click-through or cost per lead getting worse on the control. When that happens, take the hook from your best-performing challenger. Don't rewrite the whole ad.
- Based on his views on volume and learning by doing, he'd probably say the real problem is testing too few hooks, not refreshing too rarely. Make lots of hooks, test them against the control, and keep the winners.

These follow from his "use it to death and try to beat it" line, his comedian testing analogy, and his habit of reducing things to inputs and outputs. They're my inference, not his words.

**Short answer:** No. Nothing in this vault backs keeping prices flat to protect your close rate. Everything Hormozi says on pricing points toward raising them: put a much more expensive tier on top, state the price plainly, and when demand is more than you can supply, charge more. The vault has no source where he talks about an 82% close rate, so the conclusion that "82% means you're too cheap" is my extrapolation from his principles.

**What he's said (in the vault)**
- **When demand is high, raise the price.** "when you have demand, cut supply." His point is that tight supply "forces you to raise your price" unless you have "limiting beliefs" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 5:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=328s)). About a craftsman who can't keep up with orders: "raise the price and just continue to keep raising the prices until eventually become Versace" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:29:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5386s)).
- **Avoid the middle of the market.** "either sell extremely expensive stuff to a select few or sell something super cheap to everyone. The middle is where people die." ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=0s))
- **Offer a tier priced 10x higher.** "If they want to pay you more money, you should give them the opportunity to do so." The high tier "literally increases the perceived value" of your main offer ([@ 7:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=425s), [@ 7:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=456s)). In his worked example, roughly three quarters of the profit comes from the 10% who buy the expensive tier.
- **Build that tier around speed and ease, not more labor.** "take whatever the delivery time you currently have is and cut it in half." "You will always have priority." The premium buyer "is a different person" from your current customer ([@ 16:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=985s), [@ 13:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=784s)).
- **Say the price out loud in the home.** "You must confront the high price." Then "We shut up. We let them talk." ([@ 8:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=489s), [@ 8:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=521s))
- **Make more from each customer.** "do what you can control, make more from each one" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)). This line is ad copy from his book launch.
- **He wouldn't make close rate your main focus.** "if you improve your sales close rate, you would your business would grow… But I'm not talking about those improvements. Those are what I consider the sausage making" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 9:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=595s)). He'd want you looking for a change that grows the business by an order of magnitude, not protecting a percentage.

**What he's done:** At a PR firm his company invested in, he noticed that about 15% of customers bought the top package and stayed. He rebuilt the business around just that group and raised prices 10x, and email response rates went up ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:23:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4991s)).

**Where this is uncertain:**
- None of the six sources talks about home services, duct cleaning, or what close rate is "healthy."
- Much of the pricing advice comes from a 2025 video aimed at people who are just starting out. Its description also links to his own sales funnel.
- He presents being a premium "artist" and being a scaling "entrepreneur" as equally good paths. He doesn't say one is right for everyone.

**Extrapolation (not in the vault)**
From the principles above, he'd most likely say an 82% close rate means you're priced below what your buyers will pay. When almost everyone who books an inspection says yes, the market is telling you there's demand left over. The math backs this up. Take 100 inspections at your current price P, with costs at 62% of revenue, and raise prices 20%. Suppose your close rate drops from 82% to 70%:
- **Revenue:** goes from 82P to 84P.
- **Profit:** goes up about 6% if all your costs are fixed, and about 30% if they all scale with the number of jobs. Most businesses fall somewhere in between.
- **Break-even close rate:** about 68% if costs are fixed, and about 54% if they all scale with jobs.

You'd also be doing fewer jobs for more profit, which frees up crew capacity.

What he'd probably have you do:
1. Raise the base price in steps, 10–20% at a time.
2. Add a premium package priced several times higher. It could include same-week priority scheduling, a dryer-vent and coil clean, an air-quality retest, an annual maintenance plan, and a guarantee.
3. Say the price outright and stop talking.
4. Watch profit per inspection, not close rate. Keep raising prices until that number stops going up.

My own note: one practical risk is that 82% may partly come from leads who already booked through you because of a referral or a specific price you advertised. If so, test the new prices on new leads first.

**Short answer:** Mostly no on ads for now, and yes on replacements, though not the way you're probably picturing. My best read of what Hormozi would say: don't give up on door-knocking two months in, because it's the exact training he recommends. Keep knocking, do more of it, and get more money out of each door, mainly by turning repair jobs into replacement jobs. Add ads once you know a new customer pays back what the ads cost to win them. Nothing in the vault covers roofing or this exact choice, so the specific plan below is labelled as extrapolation.

**What he's said**

- **Door-to-door is where he tells people to build their sales skill, and the first three months are the hard part.** He recommends "high volume transactional sales so whether that's you doing door to door or you cold calling," because "you want quick feedback loops so that you can learn what you did wrong" ([39:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2370s)). Also: "for most people if they can weather the first three months of say sales then they'll usually be fine," and "go Shadow the best guy and do twice the volume he's doing" ([40:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2402s)). You're in month two.
- **He thinks of results as a numbers game.** "the output is that I will be a very good salesman the inputs is that I have to do I have to collect 5,000 NOS" ([47:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2868s)). At 1 sale per 20 doors, you've heard roughly 19 no's for every yes.
- **He'd push you to make more from each customer before paying more to find customers.** "do what you can control, make more from each one" ([8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)). His ad rule is "spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). He paid for the ads on one book launch out of his own pocket because "it had no offer to liquidate ad spend," meaning nothing to sell that would earn the ad money back. For the next launch he built that offer first ([7:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=465s)).
- **Bigger tickets take the same work.** "solve rich people problems they pay better" and "find the people who value what you have the most" ([1:38:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5918s)). Also: "you sell your first $10,000 thing you sell your first $100,000 thing … you realize it's the exact same thing" ([1:40:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6049s)).
- **If too few people say yes, improve the offer.** "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([1:24:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5089s)).
- **Pick one thing.** "Sometimes you have to sit with the pain of an unbuilt bridge without building a second bridge" ([4:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=298s)). Trying to solve a problem in several ways at once "ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work but will take time" ([6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)).

**What he's done:** He learned Facebook ads two weeks before opening his first gym ([1:17:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4668s)), so he isn't against ads early on. But during that first stretch he also ran sales calls himself at 8, 9, 10 and 11 p.m. for about six months ([55:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=3305s)).

**Where this is uncertain:** The vault doesn't cover roofing or home services. It also doesn't include his leads book, where his detailed ad and lead-generation advice lives. Two conflicts of interest to know about: the money-model lines come from ads for his own book, and he sells ad know-how.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the principles above, not his words)

1. **Work out where your $20k comes from.** At $1,500 a repair and about $20k a replacement, $20k a month could be one replacement or about 13 repairs. That's very different from 1 in 20 doors at full price. Hormozi would want you to know how many doors it takes to land one replacement, not just one sale of any kind.
2. **Treat repairs as the way into replacements.** This is his "make more from each one" idea. Every repair visit is a chance to inspect the roof and quote a replacement, using a planned offer and timing, such as crediting the repair cost toward a replacement within 12 months. Moving even a few repair customers up to a $20k job beats any ad budget.
3. **Make replacements the one thing, and keep door-knocking as the way you get them.** That points you at richer customers ("solve rich people problems") without starting a second sales channel before the first one is proven. Knock in neighborhoods with older roofs or recent storm damage, and aim to double your door count rather than switch channels.
4. **Run ads when the numbers say you can afford to.** Once you know your close rate on replacement quotes, you know how much you can pay for one replacement lead and still break even. A $20k ticket can carry a lot of ad spend, and that's when he'd say spend as much as you can. Running ads now, before you can sell well and before you have a strong offer, is like building a second bridge.

My one disagreement: knocking doors is seasonal and depends heavily on weather, so I'd test a small ad budget earlier than "month three or later." I'd keep it small and treat it as a way to learn what a lead costs, not as the growth plan.

From what it does contain, his advice would probably be to fix your offer and money model before you spread budget across new channels. Raise how much you make from each customer so you can afford more on Meta, and don't start two or three new bets at once. Most of this answer is extrapolation, and it's labelled below.

**What he's said (sourced)**
- **Spend as much as you can while staying at break-even or better.** "the goal is to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). He treats the limit on spend as an economics problem, not a channel problem.
- **When customers cost too much, earn more from each one.** "rather than thinking, 'Oh, I'm spending too much to get customers, do what you can control, make more from each one.'" (same video @ 8:50, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s). He says a money model exists to "pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion … so that you can scale" (@ 8:17). Caveat: these lines are ad scripts promoting his own book launch.
- **A better offer is the biggest lever.** "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" and "it's the highest leverage thing I think you can do in the business" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:24:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5089s)).
- **Don't run several fixes at once.** "me trying to solve it in two or three ways ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work but will take time" and "Sometimes you have to sit with the pain of an unbuilt bridge without building a second bridge" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s), @ 4:58). In the same talk he admits he's guilty of this himself.
- **Avoid chasing shiny new things.** "People underestimate how much effort it takes to stick with one thing rather than jumping to the next shiny opportunity every six months" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 22:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1344s)).
- **Find what's limiting the system.** "we have to identify what the constraint of the of the system is" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:30:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5419s)).

**What he's done:** He paid for the ads on his previous book launch himself because there was no offer to earn the ad spend back. For the 2025 Money Models launch he built that offer first, so he could push spend and still break even (yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 7:45). His fix was to change the economics, not to add a channel.

**Where this is uncertain**
- The vault has 6 sources, and none covers lead channels. His leads book is mentioned but not included, and it's the most likely place he deals with this directly (affiliates, getting other people to promote you, scaling ad spend). Read it before deciding.
- His point about not spreading resources thin could cut either way. If Meta really is maxed out, one new channel could be "the one thing." The vault doesn't settle this.

**Extrapolation (not sourced; built from the principles above)**
1. **Work out what the wall is first.** If your cost per customer jumps past $100k a month, it's either ad fatigue (you need new ads and hooks) or you've exhausted your audience. Hormozi would trace it back to the economics, not blame the platform.
2. **Fix the money model before moving budget.** Add upsells, a premium tier priced about 10x your main offer (see `pricing/premium/high-ticket-anchor-tier`), and front-end offers that bring cash in sooner. If each customer earns you more in the first 30 days, you can pay more per customer and still break even. Your Meta ceiling then moves from $100k to well above it.
3. **If you add a channel, add one.** Pick the single channel most likely to change the business in 12 months, give it real resources, and let smaller problems wait. Don't split budget across affiliates *and* podcasts *and* other tests at the same time.
4. **Affiliates fit his logic better than podcasts.** This is the most speculative point. Affiliates are paid per sale, so they fit his rule of spending as much as possible while breaking even. A stronger money model also means you can pay affiliates more than competitors do. Podcasts are harder to measure against break-even.
5. **Getting 85% of customers from Meta is a risk.** He lost six months of revenue when a payment processor froze his funds (from `profile`). Diversifying is a sensible hedge, but he'd probably treat it as risk management, not the fix for your growth ceiling.

My own view, separately: at your size, test one new channel properly while you fix the money model. These don't really conflict, as long as the channel gets its own small team and budget.

**Short answer:** No. Hormozi has dealt with almost exactly this situation, and he did the opposite of what you're planning. In his Skool Games community, the top cancel reason was overwhelm. He cut the calls from three a week to one and released content less often. Adding more trainings and calls makes "can't keep up" worse, and it probably won't fix "too expensive" either.

**What he's said**

- **The direct case.** He says the fix for overwhelm-driven churn isn't more value. It's more value in less time: "the number one reason that people were cancelling was overwhelm. It was not oh I need to provide more value. It was I need to provide more value per second in fewer total seconds." ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s))
- **What he changed.** "we removed two of the three calls, except kept it to one and we moved the big download from once a month to once a quarter so that people could get on top of it". He also switched off app features so new members had fewer things to do. His reason: "Oh my god, there's so many things I have to do. I can't think about it." And then they leave" ([@ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s))
- **The rule he took from it.** "you only introduce something when it's required or necessary for that person to get the the desired value". Have people do the one thing most of them find valuable first, perfect that step, then show the next one. ([@ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s))
- **The general principle.** "how much can I take away and still have it be good and not only be good but it probably is better" ([@ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s)). Adding is the lazy option: "complexity is typically the child of lazy thinking" ([@ 1:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=103s)).
- **Effort counts against value.** In his value equation, effort and sacrifice sit in the denominator: "effort are the things that you have to start doing that you don't want to do as a result of this purchase" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:21:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4864s)). Each new call or training adds to that effort.
- **Remove friction.** For premium offers he says to walk through the customer experience and "take a note every time you have to do something", then remove those steps ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 17:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=1020s)).

**What he's done:** He made the cuts above in Skool Games specifically to reduce cancellations. He didn't share before-and-after churn numbers in this source.

**Where this is uncertain**

- The vault only covers "can't keep up" directly. He never addresses "too expensive" as a cancel reason, a 30% monthly churn rate, or how to price a $99/month membership.
- The Skool example is a single anecdote from one solo talk (2025), with no retention numbers.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from his principles, not his words)

- **"Too expensive" and "can't keep up" are probably one problem.** In the value equation, price only feels too high when perceived value is low. That happens when effort is high and the member's perceived likelihood of getting the result drops, which is what falling behind does to someone. Bonus content raises effort, so by his framework it makes the membership feel *more* expensive. This is my reading of his framework; he didn't say it.
- **What he'd probably have you do, in order:**
  1. **Subtract.** Find the one call or training that most of your retained members actually use. Keep it, cut or archive the rest, and release content on a schedule people can keep up with.
  2. **Shorten the time to the first result.** He calls speed the biggest persuasion lever: "latency beats magnitude 7 days a week" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 15:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=953s)). Give new members one clear first step and a quick win in week one, when cancel risk is probably highest.
  3. **Look at your money model and your buyers, not just the content.** His line is "make more from each one" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)), and he advises finding "the people who value what you have the most" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:38:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5918s)). Check which members stay longest, aim your marketing at people like them, and consider a higher-priced tier that's faster and easier for those who want more. Don't put more volume into the base tier.
- **Test it before rolling it out.** Cut the extras for one cohort, then compare their 30- and 60-day cancellation rates against your current baseline. Ask cancelling members which parts they actually used.

My own note: "too expensive" is sometimes really about the buyer's budget, not perceived value. If your exit surveys show that, a cheaper or annual option is worth testing alongside the cuts. That part is my addition, not something from the vault.
